The equiatomic quinary baseline is expected to show similar improvements but possibly to a lesser degree if it already has optimal hydrogen uptake characteristics.
hypothesis.baseline: Standard hydrogen charging without surface passivation as performed in the equiatomic quinary baseline.
hypothesis.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where hydrogen charging (via cathodic methods) is used and where surface-induced hydrogen gradients are significant; it may not be relevant if alternative charging methods that inherently produce uniform hydrogen distributions are employed.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact impact of surface passivation on the internal hydrogen gradient and subsequent deformation behavior is less well-established; quantitative improvements may vary with coating thickness and composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical alloy samples (quinary, quaternary, and ternary) and split into two groups: one receiving the surface passivation treatment (e.g., by immersion in a passivating electrolyte or deposition of a thin inert oxide) and one without; perform identical hydrogen charging and in-situ tensile tests; examine fracture surfaces for intergranular features and map hydrogen concentration profiles near surfaces using techniques like secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) or thermal desorption; correlate these with deformation microstructures.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (SEM analysis)
Hydrogen concentration gradients (SIMS or TDA-MS)
Tensile properties (ultimate tensile strength, ductility, yield strength)
Nanotwin density uniformity (via ECCI/EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If surface passivation does not lead to a significant reduction in hydrogen concentration gradients and corresponding changes in fracture mode or deformation microstructure compared to non-passivated samples, then this hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: Magnetically-driven phase transformation strengthening in high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s evidence that in CrCoNi the fcc-to-hcp transformation is favorable at lower temperatures (via vibrational entropy analysis) and that dislocation interactions can trigger hcp nucleation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s findings by proposing a controlled processing route (cryogenic deformation) to deliberately enhance the transformation-induced strengthening mechanism, rather than relying solely on ambient deformation conditions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Deforming equiatomic CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures will enhance the dislocation-activated fcc-to-hcp transformation, increasing the population of localized hcp laths and thereby improving strength-ductility synergy relative to room-temperature processed samples.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy with a predominantly FCC structure subjected to standard thermomechanical processing.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical processing route that includes deformation at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., liquid nitrogen temperature, ~77 K) instead of room temperature deformation.
hypothesis.conditions: Conduct parallel deformation experiments under identical strain rates and strain levels (up to ~55% true strain) at cryogenic (77 K) and room temperatures, ensuring similar strain paths.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enhanced nucleation and growth of hcp nanolaths localized at stacking faults and twin interfaces.
hypothesis.mechanism: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations presented in the paper indicate that vibrational entropy contributions can tilt the phase stability in favor of the hcp phase at lower temperatures. Cryogenic deformation reduces thermal vibrations and may lower the stacking fault energy barrier, hence promoting the nucleation of hcp laths during dislocation slip. These hcp regions act as strong barriers to dislocation motion while accommodating plasticity, leading to an improved balance of strength and ductility.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Cryogenically deformed CrCoNi samples are predicted to exhibit a higher density of hcp laths (observable by STEM/COS mapping) with an increase in yield strength and work hardening compared to room-temperature deformed samples. The scale of the effect is expected to be moderate, though precise numbers are not certain.
hypothesis.baseline: CrCoNi processed and deformed at room temperature.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism applies to deformation regimes where the temperature effects significantly influence stacking fault energies; excessive cold could embrittle the alloy if deformation rates are not optimized.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative gains in mechanical properties are not fully predictable due to potential competing effects at very low temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrCoNi samples and deform them under controlled conditions at both cryogenic (77 K) and room temperatures. Use high-resolution STEM (with COS mapping) to quantify the formation of hcp nanolaths and perform standardized tensile and fatigue tests to assess mechanical performance.
measurements: Quantitative TEM analysis for hcp and twin structure density
Mechanical testing (yield strength, tensile strength, ductility)
Measurement of stacking fault energies if possible
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cryogenically deformed samples do not display a statistically significant increase in hcp lath formation and corresponding improvements in mechanical properties compared to room-temperature processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C13

source_paper.title: Deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in a CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the mechanism of dislocation pile-up and crack-tip amorphization observed in the Cantor alloy (PMC8011962) indicating that high lattice friction combined with dislocation trapping promotes amorphization.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes tailoring the grain-boundary character (especially increasing high-angle boundaries) to intentionally enhance local dislocation accumulation and phase transformation – an intervention not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In ultrafine-grained (UFG) subsets of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, increasing the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries will promote stronger dislocation accumulation and earlier localized amorphization at crack tips, thereby enhancing energy dissipation and fracture toughness.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: UFG equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni with a mixed grain-boundary character.
hypothesis.intervention: Tailor the thermomechanical processing (e.g., modifying annealing temperature/time and rolling reduction) to increase the proportion of high-angle grain boundaries versus low-angle boundaries.
hypothesis.conditions: Room-temperature deformation with controlled crack initiation under quasi-static loading; samples processed into UFG state with average grain sizes around 500 nm but varying grain-boundary misorientations.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The increased high-angle grain boundaries act as stronger barriers to dislocation slip, leading to higher local dislocation densities at crack tips.
hypothesis.mechanism: As shown in the paper, high local dislocation density near crack tips triggers crystalline-to-amorphous transformation. High-angle grain boundaries enhance dislocation pile-ups because of their stronger barrier effect. This in turn reduces the effective slip and facilitates local amorphization, thereby dissipating more energy and enhancing toughness. (See evidence in PMC8011962::web::017 and supporting discussion on grain-boundary resistance.)
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline UFG alloy with mixed boundary character, samples with a higher fraction of high-angle boundaries will exhibit a lower threshold for amorphization at crack tips, increased energy dissipation, and improved apparent fracture toughness; the effect is expected to be significant in enhancing crack-tip toughening but might reduce uniform ductility if amorphization becomes excessive.
hypothesis.baseline: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni UFG alloy processed under standard conditions as in the baseline reported in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant only in UFG microstructures where grain boundaries are closely spaced; in coarse-grained materials, the effect may be negligible.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in toughness and the optimum fraction of high-angle boundaries remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several UFG Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy samples with systematically varied grain-boundary character distributions through controlled annealing. Introduce identical notches and perform in situ TEM or fracture toughness tests to measure the onset and extent of amorphization near crack tips.
measurements: Grain-boundary misorientation mapping (e.g., EBSD) to quantify high-angle boundary fractions
In situ TEM observations of crack-tip microstructure (dislocation density and amorphous band formation)
Fracture toughness (e.g., KIC) measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries does not correlate with a lower threshold of amorphization and does not result in improved crack-tip toughening (i.e., no significant increase in fracture toughness compared to baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.
